Fourteen verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾

The connection with what precedes it: in that surah (al-Mumtahanah) there is an explanation of going forth in jihad in the way of Allah and seeking His pleasure, in His saying: ﴿If you have gone forth to strive in My way and seeking My approval﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. In this surah there is an explanation of what moves the people of faith and urges them to jihad, in His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a battle line as if they were a structure joined firmly﴾. As for the connection of the first to the last, it is as if He said: If the disbelievers, out of their ignorance, attribute to Our sacred presence what is not fitting for that presence, then the angels and others among mankind and the jinn have been glorifying Our presence, as He said: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah﴾, meaning: everything in the heavens and the earth bears witness to His lordship, His oneness, and His other praiseworthy attributes. And "al-'Aziz" is one who is mighty when he prevails; He is the One who prevails over others, whatever those others may be, and no other can prevail over Him.

And "al-Hakim" is one who judges concerning a thing when he decides it; He is the One who passes judgment over others, whatever those others may be, and no other can pass judgment over Him. So His saying: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah﴾ indicates His lordship and oneness, then. Furthermore, He, exalted is He, said in some surahs: "exalts Allah" (sabbaha), in some: "exalts" (yusabbihu), and in some: "exalt" (sabbih) in the imperative form, so that it is known that the glorification of the presence of Allah, exalted is He, is continuous and unbroken, since the past tense indicates it in past time, the future tense indicates it in future time, and the imperative indicates it in the present.

His exalted saying: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ Some have said: this verse concerns a group of believers who wished to act upon the most beloved of deeds to Allah, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I direct you to a transaction﴾ [al-Saff: 10] and "Indeed, Allah loves those who fight," but they loved life and turned away on the day of Uhud, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed:

[Page 270]
﴿why do you say what you do not do?﴾ It has also been said that it concerns the one who says "I fought" but did not fight, "I struck" but did not strike, "I did" but did not do. It has been said too that it concerns the hypocrites regarding fighting, because they wished for fighting, and when Allah, exalted is He, commanded it, they said: ﴿Why have You prescribed for us fighting?﴾ [al-Nisa: 77]. It has also been said that it concerns every believer, because they believed in fulfilling what Allah promised them of obedience, submission, humility and reverence. So when the fulfilment of what He promised them is not realised, they are feared, in every lapse, to enter into this verse. Then, in this passage, there are several discussions:

First: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah﴾ at the beginning of this surah, and He said it again at the beginning of another surah. This is repetition, and repetition is a fault; so how is it? We say: it may be said that He repeated it so that it would be known that in reality it is not repeated, because what glorified Him at the existence of the world, by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, is other than what glorified Him after the existence of the world; likewise at the existence of Adam and after his existence.

Second: He said: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah﴾ and did not say: "The heavens and the earth and what is in them exalt Allah," although there is in this more emphasis than in that? We say: that would be so only if the intended glorification were glorification by the tongue of disposition in general; but if the intended glorification is a specific glorification, then some are described thus, and so it is not as you have mentioned.

Third: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "li-ma" is the lam of attribution entering upon the interrogative "ma", as other prepositions entered upon it in your saying: "bi-ma", "fi-ma", "amma", "imma"; the alif was deleted because "ma" and the preposition are like one thing; and its use has occurred in the speech of one asking a question. Had it been so, the meaning of interrogation would apply to His saying: ﴿why do you say what you do not do?﴾, and interrogation from Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, since He knows all things. We say: this is when the intended interrogation is seeking understanding; but when the intended purpose is to hold accountable those who turned away from fulfilling what they promised, or denied the truth and persisted in falsehood, then it is not.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾

Al-maqt is al-bughd (hatred), and whoever deserves the hatred of Allah is bound to receive punishment. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, Zamakhshari's Qur'anic commentary) said: al-maqt is the most intense, most complete and most abominable hatred. Al-Zajjaj said: "an" is in the place of nominative case (raf'), and "maqtan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). The meaning is: your saying what you do not do is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is a great word﴾ [al-Kahf 18:5].

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as if they were a solid structure.﴾

Zayd ibn Ali read yuqatalun with a fatha on the ta'. It was also read yaqtulun, meaning they arrange themselves in a row (yasuffun saffan). The meaning is that they arrange themselves in battle as if they were a solid structure (bunyan marsus). Al-Farra' said: "marsus" means fastened with lead (bi'l-rasas). It is said: "I fastened the building" (rassastu al-bina') when I joined its parts together and brought them close until it becomes like a single piece. Al-Layth said: it is said "I fastened the building" when you pressed it together, and al-rass (fastening) is the joining of things to one another. Ibn Abbas said: a stone is placed upon a stone and then fastened with small stones, and then the brick is placed upon it, and the people of Makkah call this the marsus. Abu Ishaq said: Allah, Exalted is He, informs that He loves the one who stands firm in jihad and holds his place, like the firmness of a fastened builder's structure. He also said: it may be that it means their affairs become equal in fighting their enemy, until they are in unity of word and mutual allegiance, like a solid structure. It was also said: this parable was coined for steadfastness, meaning that when they stand in rows they remain firm like a solid, settled structure. It was also said: in this there is evidence of the excellence of fighting on foot, because the Arabs arrange themselves in this manner. Then, as for love in its apparent sense, it has two aspects:
First: approval of the creatures.
Second: praise of them for what they do.

Then, what is the connection of this verse with what precedes it, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that﴾? We say: that verse is a reproach of those who opposed in fighting, who were those who promised to fight but did not fight; and this verse is a commendation of those who agreed in fighting, who were those who fought in the cause of Allah and strove hard in it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 61, verses 5–7:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me when you know that I am the Messenger of God to you?" So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate, and God does not guide the defiant people.﴾

Its meaning: remember this story. The word *idh* (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied *udhkur* (remember), meaning: remember the time when he said to them, ﴿Why do you harm me?﴾ They used to harm him in various ways, by speech and by action. They said, ﴿Show us God plainly﴾ and ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾. It was also said that they accused him of having a testicular hernia (*al-udra*). His words, exalted is He, ﴿while you know that I am the Messenger of God﴾, are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: you harm me while knowing with certain knowledge that I am the Messenger of God. The fact that you know this obliges you to honor and revere me. His words ﴿So when they deviated﴾ mean they turned away towards what is other than the truth. ﴿God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ means He turned their hearts away from the truth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. Muqatil said: "﴿They deviated﴾ means they turned away from the truth with their bodies, ﴿God caused [them] to deviate﴾ means God turned their hearts away from the truth and led them astray as recompense for what they did." This is supported by His words, exalted is He, ﴿God does not guide the defiant people.﴾ Abu Ishaq said its meaning is: God does not guide those who, in His foreknowledge, are destined to be defiant. In this there is a warning about the gravity of harming the Messenger (ﷺ), to the point that it leads to disbelief and the deviation of hearts from guidance. The word *qad* here means emphasis, as if He had said: you know with certain knowledge, with no doubt on your part.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said, "O Children of Israel, I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and bringing good news of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is plain magic."﴾ ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God while he is being invited to Islam? God does not guide the unjust people.﴾

His words ﴿I am the Messenger of God﴾ mean: remember that I have been sent to you with the description by which I was described in the Torah. ["Confirming"] means confirming the Torah, and the books of God, and all His prophets, those who came before and those who came after. ﴿And bringing good news of a Messenger﴾ who confirms the Torah in the same way as I confirm it. It is as if it was said to him: what is his name? So he said: his name is Ahmad. His words ﴿who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ are two clauses in the genitive position, because they are two descriptors of the indefinite noun *rasul* (messenger). In ﴿after me, his name﴾ there are two readings: vowelling the *ya'* with a *fatha*, which is the original form and is the preferred view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh in every position where the *ya'* is dropped due to the meeting of two unvoweled letters. And its being unvoweled, as in His words, ﴿and for whoever enters my house﴾ [Nuh: 28]. Whoever reads it unvoweled in ﴿min ba'di ismuhu﴾ drops the *ya'* and the *sin* from his name. This is what al-Mubarrad and Abu Ali said. His words, exalted is He, ﴿Ahmad﴾ may have two meanings:

The first: intensification in the agent, meaning that he praises God more than anyone else does.

The second: intensification in the patient, meaning that he is praised for his sincerity and good character more than anyone else is praised.

Now let us mention some of what Jesus, peace be upon him, brought concerning the coming of our master Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the Gospel, in several places:

The first: in the fourteenth chapter of the Gospel of John, as follows: "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, that he may abide with you forever, the Farqalit (Paraclete), who is the Spirit of truth." This is the wording of the Gospel as translated into Arabic. And in the fifteenth chapter, he mentioned this wording: "But the Farqalit, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of all that I have told you." Then after a little, he mentioned: "And I have told you this before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe."

The second: he mentioned in the sixteenth chapter as follows: "But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Farqalit will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment."

The third: he mentioned after that, a little later, as follows: "I have much more to say to you, but you cannot bear it now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority."

This is what is in the Gospel. If it is said: the meaning of the Farqalit is that when he comes he will guide them to the truth and teach them the Law, and that this was Jesus, who came after the crucifixion? We say: the disciples mentioned at the end of the Gospel that when Jesus came after the crucifixion, he did not mention any part of the Law, nor did he teach them any of the rulings. He did not stay with them except for a moment, and he spoke only a little, such as when he said: "I am the Messiah, so do not think that I am dead; rather, I am saved with God, watching over you. And I am not inspired after this to you." This is the complete statement.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿But when he came to them with clear proofs﴾: it has been said that this refers to Jesus, and it has been said that it refers to Muhammad. The phrase indicates that the one who came to them with clear proofs came with miracles and clear signs that show that what he brought was from God. His words, exalted is He, ﴿This is plain magic﴾ mean: "This is a plain magician." His words ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾ mean: who is more grievously unjust than one whose fabrication has reached the point of inventing lies against God, while they knew that whatever blessing and honor they received came from God, exalted is He, and then they disbelieved in Him and lied against God and His Messenger. ﴿God does not guide the unjust people﴾ means God does not grant them success in obedience, as a punishment for them.

There is a discussion concerning the verse: it may be asked, with what is ﴿muṣaddiqan﴾ and ﴿mubashshiran﴾ in the accusative: is it governed by the meaning of "sending" contained in "messenger", or by "to you"? We say: rather, it is governed by the meaning of "sending", because "to you" is a complement of "messenger".

Third: light is like knowledge, and darkness is like ignorance. Or light is faith, which brings them out of darknesses into light. Or Islam is the light. Then, the benefits of its being a light are several aspects:

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى:

﴿Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu, hal adullukum ʿala tijaratin tunjikum min ʿadhabin alim?﴾ ("O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?") ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi wa tujahidina fi sabilillahi bi-amwalikum wa anfusikum, dhalikum khayrun lakum in kuntum taʿlamun.﴾ ("You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew.")

Know that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿hal adullukum﴾ ("shall I guide you"), is in the sense of a command according to al-Farra' (the grammarian). It is said: "Hal anta samitun" ("Are you silent?"), meaning: "Be silent." Its explanation: *hal* is in the sense of a question, then it gradually becomes an offer and an urging, and urging is like inciting, and inciting is a command.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿ʿala tijaratin﴾ ("to a transaction"): it is the trade between the people of faith and the presence of Allah, Exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi﴾ indicates this. *Tijarah* (trade) is an expression for the exchange of one thing for another. Just as trade saves the merchant from the trial of poverty, and the reward of patience with what accompanies it, so this trade, which is the affirmation by the heart and the declaration by the tongue, as is said in the definition of faith, saves the believer. Therefore He said it with the word *tijarah*. And just as trade involves profit and loss, so it is in this matter: whoever believes and does righteous deeds has the reward, abundant profit and clear prosperity, and whoever turns away from righteous deeds has regret and clear loss.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿tunjikum min ʿadhabin alim﴾ ("will save you from a painful punishment") is read with a light and a heavy (intensive) form. ﴿Tu'minuna﴾ is a resumptive sentence, as if they had said: "How should we act?" So He said: ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi﴾, and it is a statement in the sense of a command. For this reason it is answered by His saying: ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ ("He will forgive you for you") and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa tujahidina fi sabilillahi﴾ ("and strive in the cause of Allah"). *Jihad* (striving) after these two aspects is of three kinds: jihad between a person and himself, which is the subduing of the self and restraining it from pleasures and desires; jihad between a person and the creation, which is that he leaves off greed toward them, and is compassionate and merciful to them; and jihad between a person and the world, which is that he takes it as provision for a journey, so this has five aspects.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿dhalikum khayrun lakum﴾ ("that is better for you") means: that which you have been commanded with, of faith in Allah, Exalted is He, and striving in His cause, is better for you than that you follow your desires. ﴿In kuntum taʿlamun﴾ ("if you knew") means: if you benefit from what you have done, then it is good for you.

In the verse there are several discussions:

The first: Why did He say ﴿tu'minuna﴾ in the form of a statement? We say: to indicate that obedience is obligatory. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (رضي الله عنه) that they said: "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, Exalted is He, we would do them." So this verse was revealed. They remained for as long as Allah willed, saying: "Would that we knew what they are!" So Allah guided them to them by His saying: ﴿tu'minuna billahi﴾.

The second: What is the meaning of ﴿in kuntum taʿlamun﴾ ("if you knew")? We say: "If you know that it is good for you, it has been good for you." These are the aspects of *al-Kashshaf*. As for others, they said: the fear is of the punishment itself, not of the painful punishment, since the painful punishment is the punishment itself together with something else, and fear is among its necessary consequences, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Al ʿImran: 175].

Among them: how is the command to faith after His saying ﴿O you who have believed﴾? We say: it is possible that the intended people in this verse are the hypocrites, who believed outwardly. It is possible that they are the People of the Book, the Jews and Christians, for they believed in the earlier scriptures, so it is as if He said: "O you who have believed in the earlier scriptures, believe in Allah and in Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah." It is possible that they are the people of faith, as in His saying: ﴿so it increased them in faith﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124] and ﴿that they may increase in faith﴾ [al-Fath: 4]. ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى:

﴿Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu, hal adullukum ʿala tijaratin tunjikum min ʿadhabin alim?﴾ ("O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?") ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi wa tujahidina fi sabilillahi bi-amwalikum wa anfusikum, dhalikum khayrun lakum in kuntum taʿlamun.﴾ ("You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew.")

Know that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿hal adullukum﴾ ("shall I guide you"), is in the sense of a command according to al-Farra' (the grammarian). It is said: "Hal anta samitun" ("Are you silent?"), meaning: "Be silent." Its explanation: *hal* is in the sense of a question, then it gradually becomes an offer and an urging, and urging is like inciting, and inciting is a command.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿ʿala tijaratin﴾ ("to a transaction"): it is the trade between the people of faith and the presence of Allah, Exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi﴾ indicates this. *Tijarah* (trade) is an expression for the exchange of one thing for another. Just as trade saves the merchant from the trial of poverty, and the reward of patience with what accompanies it, so this trade, which is the affirmation by the heart and the declaration by the tongue, as is said in the definition of faith, saves the believer. Therefore He said it with the word *tijarah*. And just as trade involves profit and loss, so it is in this matter: whoever believes and does righteous deeds has the reward, abundant profit and clear prosperity, and whoever turns away from righteous deeds has regret and clear loss.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿tunjikum min ʿadhabin alim﴾ ("will save you from a painful punishment") is read with a light and a heavy (intensive) form. ﴿Tu'minuna﴾ is a resumptive sentence, as if they had said: "How should we act?" So He said: ﴿Tu'minuna billahi wa rasulihi﴾, and it is a statement in the sense of a command. For this reason it is answered by His saying: ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ ("He will forgive you for you") and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa tujahidina fi sabilillahi﴾ ("and strive in the cause of Allah"). *Jihad* (striving) after these two aspects is of three kinds: jihad between a person and himself, which is the subduing of the self and restraining it from pleasures and desires; jihad between a person and the creation, which is that he leaves off greed toward them, and is compassionate and merciful to them; and jihad between a person and the world, which is that he takes it as provision for a journey, so this has five aspects.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿dhalikum khayrun lakum﴾ ("that is better for you") means: that which you have been commanded with, of faith in Allah, Exalted is He, and striving in His cause, is better for you than that you follow your desires. ﴿In kuntum taʿlamun﴾ ("if you knew") means: if you benefit from what you have done, then it is good for you.

In the verse there are several discussions:

The first: Why did He say ﴿tu'minuna﴾ in the form of a statement? We say: to indicate that obedience is obligatory. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (رضي الله عنه) that they said: "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, Exalted is He, we would do them." So this verse was revealed. They remained for as long as Allah willed, saying: "Would that we knew what they are!" So Allah guided them to them by His saying: ﴿tu'minuna billahi﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 61, verses 12–13:

Then He, exalted is He, said:

﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in the Gardens of Eden. That is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿And another favour you love: help from Allah and a near victory. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾

Know that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ is the answer (jawab) to His statement ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah﴾, because it carries the meaning of a command, as has passed. So it is as if He said: "Believe in Allah and strive in the way of Allah; He will forgive you." It has also been said that its answer is ﴿That is better for you﴾, and ﴿He will forgive you﴾ is in the jussive (majzum) form because it is a restatement (tarjamah) of ﴿That is better for you﴾. Its place is jussive, like His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Had You delayed me to a near term, I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10], because the place of ﴿I would give charity﴾ is jussive upon His statement ﴿Had You delayed me﴾. It has been said that ﴿He will forgive you﴾ is jussive by virtue of ﴿hal﴾ (a shortened form of an interrogative used here as an exhortation), because it carries the meaning of a command.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ to the end of the verse, is among what was previously explained in the Torah. It is not far-fetched to say that Allah, exalted is He, encouraged them in this verse to leave their dwellings, spend their wealth, and fight, and this is His statement ﴿He will forgive you﴾. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿That is the great triumph﴾ means: that recompense, which is everlasting, is the great triumph, as has already passed.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and another favour you love﴾ means another trade, in this world, along with the reward of the next. Al-Farra' said: "And another quality you love in this world, along with the reward of the Hereafter." His statement, exalted is He, ﴿help from Allah﴾ explains the "another," because it is fitting that ﴿help from Allah﴾ be an explanation of the trade, since help is not a trade for us; rather it is the profit of the trade. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and a near victory﴾ means imminent, and it is the conquest of Mecca. Al-Hasan said: it is the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. In ﴿you love﴾ there is a measure of rebuke for loving the worldly, immediate things.

Then, in the verse, there are discussions:

The first: His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So give good tidings to the believers﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon ﴿You believe﴾, because it carries the meaning of a command. It is as if it were said: "Believe and strive; Allah will reward you and grant you victory. And, O Messenger of Allah, give good tidings to the believers of this." It is also said: On what is the accusative of the one who read ﴿help from Allah and a near victory﴾ (nasran min Allah wa fathan qariban) based? It is said: it is accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), or upon "you will be helped with help," or "He will grant you a conquest," or upon "He will forgive you, and admit you, and give you good," or "He will show help and conquest." This is how it is mentioned in al-Kashshaf.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 61, verse 14:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah."﴾

His saying: ﴿Be helpers of Allah﴾ means: by continuing in the help and steadfastness upon it, i.e., persist in what you are upon of help. This is indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Be you (yourselves) helpers of Allah," so that He informs about them with that, i.e., helpers of the religion of Allah. His saying: ﴿as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples﴾ means: help the religion of Allah like the help of the disciples when he said to them, ﴿Who are my helpers for Allah?﴾ Muqatil said: meaning, who will protect me from Allah? Ata' said: who will help the religion of Allah? Some said: Allah commanded the believers to help Muhammad ﷺ as the disciples helped Jesus, peace be upon him. In this is an indication that help through jihad is not restricted to this Ummah. The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were his chosen ones and the first to believe in him, and they were twelve men. The hawari of a man is his chosen friend and sincere companion, from al-hawar, which is pure whiteness. It was also said: they were launderers who whitened (yuhawwirun) clothes, i.e., they made them white.

As for the helpers (ansar), Qatadah said: all the helpers were from Quraysh: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Hamzah, Ja'far, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Uthman ibn Maz'un, Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Uthman ibn 'Affan, Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, and al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam.

Then in the verse there are discussions:

The first discussion: The comparison is carried over to the meaning, and what is intended is: be as the disciples were.

The second: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers for Allah?﴾ We say: its meaning must correspond to the answer of the disciples, and what corresponds to it is that the meaning be: who is a soldier heading toward the help of Allah? The idafa in "ansari" (my helpers) differs from the idafa in "ansar Allah" (helpers of Allah), because the meaning in the first is: those who help Allah, and in the second: those who are specifically with me and are with me in the help of Allah.

The third: The companions of Jesus said, "We are helpers of Allah," and the companions of Muhammad ﷺ did not say so. We say: the address of Jesus, peace be upon him, was by way of a question, so the answer is binding; the address of Muhammad ﷺ was by way of a command, so the answer is not binding. Rather, what is binding is compliance with this command, which is His saying: ﴿Be helpers of Allah.﴾

* Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became the ones who prevailed.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: it means those who believed in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him, and those who disbelieved likewise. That is because when Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised to the heaven, they split into three groups: one group said: he was God, and God ascended; a second group said: he was the son of God, and God raised him to Himself; and a third group said: he was the servant of God and His messenger, and God raised him to Himself. These were the Muslims. Each group was followed by a section of people, and the two disbelieving groups united against the believing group, so they killed them and drove them out in the land. The situation remained so until Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ, and the believing group prevailed over the disbelieving group. That is His saying: ﴿Then We supported those who believed against their enemy.﴾ Mujahid said: "they became the ones who prevailed" means those who followed Jesus, and this is the saying of the two Muqatils. According to this view, the meaning of the verse is that those who believed in Jesus prevailed over those who disbelieved in him, and they became dominant over the people of the religions. Ibrahim said: the proof of those who believed in Jesus became manifest through the confirmation of Muhammad ﷺ and that Jesus is the Word of Allah and His Spirit. Al-Kalbi said: prevailing by proof. The prevailing by proof is the saying of Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. And Allah knows best what is correct. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and all his companions.
